The white mycelial growth at the soil line and crown rot pattern is strongly suggestive of **Southern Blight** (Sclerotium rolfsii). Let me view a reference image to confirm.

**Key observations from the test image:**
- **Affected area**: Crown/stem base at soil line — the stem has been split longitudinally
- **White mycelial growth**: Visible at the soil line/crown, pale white coating on the exterior of the stem base
- **Crown rot**: Internal stem tissue exposed showing necrosis
- **Complete plant death**: Brown, desiccated wilted foliage and root system
- **Sandy soil context**: Plant pulled from sandy/dry soil

**Differential reasoning:**
- **Southern Blight** (Sclerotium rolfsii): Characteristic white mycelial fan at the soil line, crown/stem rot starting at ground level, rapid plant collapse — this matches perfectly
- **Sclerotinia Timber Rot**: Also white mycelium, but typically higher on stem with larger black sclerotia inside stem cavities
- **Verticillium Wilt**: Would show vascular browning in cut stem cross-section, no white external mycelium
- **Southern Bacterial Wilt**: Bacterial streaming when cut, no white fungal growth

The combination of white mycelial growth specifically at the soil line, crown rot with stem splitting, and rapid whole-plant death is the hallmark presentation of Southern Blight caused by Sclerotium rolfsii.
